subtitle: Practice reading what your division rewards, recognizes and tolerates, sending clearer signals, listening at scale without exposing anyone, and changing culture one routine at a time with the people it affects.
audience: For senior leaders, directors and managers of managers who are responsible for the culture of a whole division or large unit, and for anyone preparing to lead at that scale.

lessons.title: What this division rewards in practice
objectives: Compare a division's stated values with what it recognizes, resources and tolerates in practice.
Identify at least two kinds of work your division tends to overlook when it celebrates success.
Describe how fairness in outcomes, processes and communication applies to recognition and assignments.
Distinguish reviewing division-wide patterns from rating or ranking individual staff.
lessons.teaching:
Culture is what people learn from what actually happens around them. Staff watch which work is praised at all-staff meetings, which requests get budget and which shortcuts nobody questions. Those patterns teach more than any values statement. In a division, they are set less by what the senior leader says than by what the senior leader recognizes, resources and tolerates, often without noticing.

A useful first step is to compare the stated values with three plain lists. What did we recognize last year, in awards, praise and announcements? What did we resource, in staff time, budget and leadership attention? What did we tolerate, such as late answers to partners, meetings where the same people always speak, or rushed decisions that skipped the people affected? Put each list beside the values the division publishes and ask where they match and where they do not. Keep each list short and concrete; three or four items is enough to start an honest conversation with your managers.

Deloitte's research on inclusive leadership treats fairness as more than identical treatment. It looks at fair outcomes, fair processes and clear communication about decisions, and it names promotions, rewards and work assignments as places where personal and process bias show up. At division scale, ask who is affected by what you reward. Whose work is missing from what you celebrate, perhaps because it is slow, relational or done with partners? How would you find out without relying only on the people already closest to leadership?

Start with your own defaults. Many leaders learned to reward speed, visible output and confidence in meetings because those were rewarded for them. They can be good things, and they can also hide careful work, partnership with people who receive services, and contributions from staff who work differently. Look at patterns across the division, never at individuals. Promotion, pay and selection decisions stay with Human Resources and its processes; your part is the signals around them. Ask a few colleagues outside your usual circle what they think the division rewards, and listen for what surprises you.
lessons.keyPoint: A division learns its real values from what its leaders recognize, resource and tolerate. Compare those three lists with what you say you value before you write another values statement.
lessons.example: Practice case: Tomasz is deputy director over waiver policy in disability services. The division's values say that people who receive services shape the work. At the last three all-staff meetings, recognition went to teams that cleared backlogs fastest. A team that spent six months redesigning a notice with self-advocates was not mentioned, and its request for paid advisor time was cut. Imani, who manages that team, raises it with Tomasz and brings examples.
lessons.question: What should Tomasz do first?
choices: Add a recognition category for partnership work at the next all-staff meeting, name Imani's team as its first recipient and ask managers for nominations.
Review with his managers what last year's recognition, funding and tolerated shortcuts said, set it beside the values, and pick one gap to close.
Thank Imani, restate the values at the next all-staff meeting and ask his managers to recognize partnership work more often.
feedback: Recognizing the team is welcome, but a new award alone leaves the funding cut and the pattern behind it untouched. Other overlooked work may stay invisible.
This is the strongest start. It treats Imani's example as evidence of a pattern, looks at all three signals together and leads to a specific change the division can keep.
Restating the values is sincere but adds words, not change. Staff will still judge the values by what is funded and praised, and Imani's concern stays unanswered.
lessons.reflection: What did you personally praise or fund in the last month? What would a new staff member conclude your division values from that alone?
lessons.action: Before your next leadership meeting, list what you recognized, resourced and let slide in the past quarter. Put the lists beside your division's stated values and mark one place where they do not match.

check.question: A division wants to know whether its culture matches its stated values. Which evidence tells it the most?
check.correct: What it has recognized, funded and tolerated over the past year, set beside the values.
wrong: How strongly managers say they agree with the values when asked at a leadership retreat.
Whether every unit has posted the values statement and discussed it at a team meeting.
check.feedback: Culture shows in practice. Agreement with the values and visible statements matter less than what leaders actually reward, resource and let pass, which is what staff watch and learn from.

lessons.title: The signals a senior leader sends every week
objectives: Identify the signals your attention, decisions and visibility choices send across a division.
Contrast how being heard before a decision looks as a Minimization, an Acceptance and an Adaptation practice.
Describe two ways to widen whose knowledge is heard before a division-level decision.
Distinguish a leader's influence on visibility from Human Resources selection decisions.
lessons.teaching:
Senior leaders send signals whether or not they mean to. What you ask about in meetings tells managers what matters. What you fund, delay or cut tells them what is real. Who briefs executives or leads cross-division work tells staff what kind of person gets ahead here, and who is heard before a decision tells them whose knowledge counts. Small choices add up, because a whole division is watching them.

Minnesota Management and Budget's leader competency guide describes how leaders send signals across a whole organization. At its in-progress stage, a leader shares successes with a key group only and relies on limited data sources without seeking diverse opinions. A proficient leader builds trust through follow-through and transparent communication, and draws on feedback from collaborators and community leaders. Each of these can be checked against your own calendar and decisions.

The intercultural continuum can describe an organization's practices, not only personal growth. IDI, LLC describes its orientations, and Milton Bennett's developmental model adds Integration. A Minimization practice sounds fair: anyone may speak at the briefing, and the same fast question-and-answer format is used for all. An Acceptance practice notices that the format favors people who think aloud quickly, already know the executives and need no interpreter or reading time. An Adaptation practice changes the routine, with materials sent early, written questions accepted, interpreters booked by default and authors briefing their own work. An Integration practice makes moving between ways of contributing an ordinary part of planning and deciding.

To read your own signals, look at a month of your calendar, your last few budget decisions and who has briefed executives or led cross-division work, by unit and role, not person by person. Ask what you are treating as normal and where you learned it. Selection and promotion follow Human Resources processes; your part is who gets the experience and visibility those processes later count. Then ask a few people who rarely brief executives what it would take for them to do so, choose one format to change, and tell people why.
lessons.keyPoint: Staff read a senior leader's calendar, budget and choice of presenters as the real values statement. Changing how opportunity is offered sends a stronger signal than any speech.
lessons.example: Practice case: Graciela directs a division that works with county human services agencies. Each month two of her managers brief the commissioner's office in a fast question-and-answer format, with no materials sent ahead. Program leads write most of the analysis the managers present. One of them, Kwame, is Deaf and works with interpreters, who are rarely booked for these briefings. Recent survey comments say the same voices are always the ones heard.
lessons.question: What should Graciela do?
choices: Invite Kwame to present his own analysis at next month's briefing, and make sure an interpreter is booked for that session.
Keep the current presenters, since the briefings go well, credit the program leads by name on every slide and invite them to observe the briefings.
Rotate presenters on criteria shared in advance, send materials ahead, book interpreters by default and let authors brief their own work.
feedback: A kind gesture, but it fixes one meeting for one person and leaves the format, and whose voice it favors, unchanged. It can also put Kwame on display.
Credit matters and is a real improvement. Yet the people who do the analysis stay out of the room, so the signal about who gets heard does not change.
This is the strongest response. It changes the routine rather than one invitation, so access and visibility no longer depend on who already has the role.
lessons.reflection: In the last month, which roles and units reached senior leaders directly, and which arrived through someone else? What habit of yours shaped that?
lessons.action: Review the last three months of your calendar and leadership briefings. Note which units, roles and ways of contributing appear, then change one format so more people can bring their own work forward.

check.question: Which description of a division's executive briefings reflects an Adaptation practice?
check.correct: Authors brief their own work, with materials, written questions and interpreters arranged ahead.
wrong: Anyone may speak, and the same fast question-and-answer format is used for every briefing.
Leaders agree that the format favors quick talkers and plan to discuss it at a retreat.
check.feedback: Using one format for everyone can favor one style. Noticing that is a real step. Adaptation goes further: it changes the routine itself and then checks whether it worked.

lessons.title: Listening at scale without exposing anyone
objectives: Explain how the enterprise engagement survey protects respondents and what its results are not used for.
Plan a way to discuss results with staff that does not try to trace any comment to a person.
Describe how stay conversations can add themes without creating records about individuals.
Draft a short report back that states what will change, what will not and why.
lessons.teaching:
A division cannot learn what working there is like only from whoever speaks up most. Engagement surveys, stay conversations and the concerns people raise each show part of the picture. Each also carries a risk that someone feels exposed. Listening at scale means gathering enough to see patterns while keeping every individual safe. It also means people can see what happened as a result.

Minnesota Management and Budget's FAQ for the 2025 enterprise engagement and inclusion survey sets out its protections. Only the unit that runs the survey knows who answered. Information that could identify a respondent is private under state data practices law. Groups with fewer than 10 respondents are combined with larger ones. Results are not used to evaluate individual managers or employees, and the survey is not a way to report misconduct; that goes to Human Resources or as agency policy provides. MMB recommends that leaders share results with employees and build action plans with them.

Carry the survey's privacy protections into how you lead. Read results by question and group, and never try to work out who wrote a comment; a distinctive comment can identify someone even without a name. If a theme points at one team, look at its routines, not at who said what. Stay conversations, in which supervisors ask what keeps people and what might lead them to leave, can add depth when supervisors bring back themes, not names, and nobody keeps notes about named individuals. Washington State's enterprise leadership competencies ask leaders to remove fear from organizational culture, and how you handle what you hear is where staff decide whether that is true.

Return what you heard, and say what you will do about it. Within a set time, tell people what you learned, what you will do, what you will not do and why, and when you will report again. Ask who was not heard, such as night shifts, remote staff, people using another language or access method, or units with few respondents. If a comment describes discrimination, harassment or a safety risk, route it to Human Resources or the equal opportunity office. A report back that admits limits builds more trust than a promise that cannot be kept.
lessons.keyPoint: Listening at scale works when people can see that speaking was safe and useful. Protect every individual, look for patterns, and tell people what you heard and what you will do.
lessons.example: Practice case: Mariam is deputy director over licensing in disability services. In this year's survey, one licensing unit of about 20 staff scored low on inclusion items, and several written comments describe meetings where questions are brushed aside. Paolo, a manager in another area, suggests matching the comments to people in the unit so each concern can be handled directly. The unit's manager is worried and asks Mariam what happens next.
lessons.question: What should Mariam do?
choices: Share the unit's themes with its staff, hold listening sessions led by someone outside the reporting line, and report back within a month.
Ask the unit's manager to meet each staff member privately to learn what is behind the comments and resolve the concerns.
Wait for the next survey cycle to see whether the pattern holds before acting, so the unit is not singled out on the strength of one result.
feedback: This is the strongest response. It treats the result as a pattern, keeps individuals unexposed, offers a safer way to add detail and shows that speaking up led somewhere.
One-to-one meetings can feel like a search for the authors, especially with the manager the comments describe. People may say less next time, and trust in the survey drops.
Caution about one result is reasonable, but a long silence tells staff their answers changed nothing. A modest, honest response now keeps the next survey worth answering.
lessons.reflection: When you have said something honest at work, what told you it was safe and worth it? What will your staff see from you after the next survey?
lessons.action: Find your division's most recent engagement survey results. Choose one theme and draft a short note to staff saying what you heard, what you will do, what you will not do and why, and when you will report back.

check.question: A senior leader receives division survey comments. Which use matches how the enterprise survey is meant to work?
check.correct: Looking for themes across groups and building an action plan with the staff who answered.
wrong: Using comments about one manager's meetings as evidence in that manager's performance review.
Sharing every written comment word for word with all staff so that nothing is filtered.
check.feedback: Minnesota Management and Budget's FAQ says results are not used to evaluate individual managers or employees, and misconduct goes to Human Resources rather than through the survey. Themes and shared action plans are the intended use. Sharing comments verbatim can identify people even without names.

lessons.title: Changing culture one routine at a time
objectives: Select one division routine where stated values and daily practice clearly differ, and plan its redesign.
Plan how the staff, partners and people served who use that routine will help redesign it.
Define what you will look at, for whom and when, to check whether the change worked.
Identify when a culture change needs Human Resources or labor relations involved.
lessons.teaching:
Culture changes through routines, not announcements. A values campaign, a slogan or a long list of initiatives rarely outlasts the leader who launched it. A changed routine, such as how work is assigned, how a meeting runs or how a partner's question gets answered, changes what people do every week. Over time, what people do becomes what the division is. Leaders often reach for visible launches because they show commitment quickly; the harder work is changing the ordinary steps people repeat.

The United States Office of Personnel Management built a federal inclusion measure on the idea that repeated behaviors form inclusive habits. Its 2017 report, now historical, said individual behaviors repeated over time create an inclusive work environment, and grouped those habits as fair, open, cooperative, supportive and empowering. The point still holds. Pick one structure where the gap between stated values and practice is clear and widely felt, and change that first. Choose one whose change people would notice within weeks.

Involve the people the routine affects before you redesign it. Ask frontline staff, partners and, where it fits, people who receive services how it works for them now and what would make it better. Decide together what you will look at, for whom and when. Their knowledge of where the routine breaks is often the best evidence you have, and involving them is itself a signal about whose experience counts. Minnesota Management and Budget's leader competency guide describes expert organizational leaders as explaining the change, monitoring results and adjusting plans. Its expert description for leading others adds disrupting norms and patterns that keep inequities in place.

Stay with a change long enough to see what it did. Most changes feel awkward for months and fade when leaders move to the next priority. Review at the times you set: what happened, for whom, and what will you keep, change or stop? Write the new routine into procedures and handover notes so it belongs to the function, not to one champion. Tell staff and partners what you learned at each review, including what did not work. Where a change touches duties, schedules or anything a labor agreement covers, bring in Human Resources and labor relations early.
lessons.keyPoint: Change one routine at a time, with the people it affects, and stay with it long enough to see what happened and for whom. A routine written into how the division works outlasts any campaign.
lessons.example: Practice case: Beatriz directs a disability services area that works with lead agencies across the state. Last year the area launched five culture initiatives, and most faded within months. Lead agency partners still say their questions wait weeks and get different answers from different staff. Sunil, a program consultant, keeps an informal answer guide that colleagues quietly rely on. A reorganization is expected next spring. Beatriz is now setting priorities for next year.
lessons.question: What should Beatriz plan for next year?
choices: Launch a refreshed set of initiatives with a values campaign and a culture committee, backed by stronger communication.
Redesign how partner questions are answered with consultants and lead agency partners, build on Sunil's guide and check at six months.
Pause culture work until the coming reorganization settles, then start again next year with a clear plan once the new structures are known.
feedback: Fresh energy and better communication help, but repeating a pattern that faded last year is likely to fade again, and partners' daily experience stays the same.
This is the strongest plan. It picks one routine partners feel, involves the people who use it, builds on knowledge already there and sets a time to check results.
Waiting can feel prudent, but the delays continue meanwhile, and staff learn that culture work stops whenever something else is busy. A focused change can start now.
lessons.reflection: Which routine in your area would show your stated values most clearly if it changed? What has kept you from changing it so far?
lessons.action: Choose one routine in your area where practice and stated values differ. This week, ask three people who use it how it works for them, then write down what you will change, what you will check and when you will review it.

check.question: Which approach is most likely to change a division's culture over time?
check.correct: Redesigning one routine with the people it affects and reviewing what happened at set times.
wrong: Launching several initiatives at once so that staff can see a strong commitment to culture.
Announcing a clear set of values and asking every manager to model them consistently.
check.feedback: Culture follows what people repeatedly do. A changed routine, designed with those affected and reviewed honestly, shifts daily practice. Announcements and many parallel initiatives tend to fade.

cards.back: A shortcut or habit leaders see and let pass, such as late answers to partners. What a division tolerates teaches staff as much as what it praises.
The patterns people learn from what leaders actually recognize, resource and tolerate. Staff read these signals more closely than any statement.
Any choice a leader makes that staff read as a message about what matters: what you ask about, fund, delay, praise or let pass.
A planned talk in which a supervisor asks what keeps a person in their job and what might lead them to leave, shared upward as themes, never names.
Telling the people who gave feedback what you heard, what you will do, what you will not do and why, and when you will update them again.

aid.heading: Read what your division rewards
items: List what you recognized last quarter: awards, praise and who presented to executives.
List what you resourced: staff time, budget requests approved and your own attention.
List what you tolerated: slow answers to partners and meetings few people can join.
Set all three beside the stated values and mark where they match and where they do not.
Look at patterns across units and groups, never at ratings of individual staff.

aid.heading: Listen without exposing anyone
items: Read survey results by question and group; never try to work out who wrote a comment.
Ask supervisors to bring themes from stay conversations, not names or notes about people.
Send discrimination, harassment or safety concerns to Human Resources or the equal opportunity office.
Ask who was not heard, such as night shifts, remote staff or units with few respondents.
Report back within a set time: what you heard, will do, will not do and why.

aid.heading: Change one routine and stay with it
items: Pick one routine where the gap between values and practice is clear and widely felt.
Redesign it with the staff, partners and people served who use it.
Decide what you will look at, for whom and when, before you start.
Review at those times and decide what to keep, change or stop.
Write the routine into procedures, and involve Human Resources and labor relations where duties change.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget, 2025 Enterprise Employee Engagement and Inclusion Survey: Frequently Asked Questions
sources.note: Supports lesson 3 on survey privacy, combining groups under 10, no use for individual evaluations, misconduct going to Human Resources, and sharing results with staff. Describes the 2025 survey only.

sources.title: Deloitte University Press, The six signature traits of inclusive leadership (2016)
sources.note: Supports lesson 1 on fairness in outcomes, processes and communication, and on promotions, rewards and assignments as places bias appears. 2016 consulting research based on interviews with leaders in six countries, mostly outside government.

sources.title: Washington State Department of Enterprise Services, Washington State Enterprise Leadership Competencies (2025)
sources.note: Supports lesson 3's reference to leaders removing fear from organizational culture. Another state's leadership model, cited as an example of an expectation, not as a Minnesota requirement.

sources.title: U.S. Office of Personnel Management, 2017 Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey Governmentwide Management Report
sources.note: Supports lesson 4's statement that repeated behaviors form inclusive habits, and the five habits named. A historical federal measure from 2017; pages on the inclusion measure only were read.

sources.title: IDI, LLC, The Intercultural Development Inventory
sources.note: Supports lesson 2's reference to the intercultural continuum orientations the IDI describes. Used here only to describe organizational practices; no assessment or result is involved or implied.

sources.title: Bennett, M. J., Towards Ethnorelativism: A Developmental Model of Intercultural Sensitivity, IDR Institute
sources.note: Supports lesson 2's use of Integration, the far point of the continuum, drawn from Bennett's developmental model. Applied here to routines and systems, never to people.
